title: Are free-scoring Brighton genuine title contenders?
summary: Are free-scoring Brighton genuine title contenders? - Published When Jack Hinshelwood unapologetically smashed home Brighton and Hove Albion's fifth goal of the game against bitter rivals Crystal Palace on Sunday, it completed a fourth straight Premier League win for the high-flying Seagulls - with ...
content:
Are free-scoring Brighton genuine title contenders?
- Published
When Jack Hinshelwood unapologetically smashed home Brighton and Hove Albion's fifth goal of the game against bitter rivals Crystal Palace on Sunday, it completed a fourth straight Premier League win for the high-flying Seagulls - with an aggregate scoreline of 15-0.
Hinshelwood's volley from two yards out to wrap up a 5-0 victory was in stark contrast to his team-mate Diego Gomez's audacious effort from the halfway line that put Brighton two up in just the seventh minute of the A23 derby.
Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring side have arguably been the most entertaining top-flight team to watch this season, but they have backed up their attacking flair with a robust defence. No team has scored more and no team has conceded fewer goals.
After seven games, they sit third on 16 points behind reigning champions Arsenal and table-toppers Manchester City, who have a 100% record. But can the Seagulls maintain their momentum and mount a serious title challenge?
"Why not?"
That's the opinion of Match of the Day pundit Dion Dublin, who played in Manchester United's 1992-93 title-winning side. "Because what we've seen of them this season is just togetherness, harmony... the manager's making good decisions.
"[Pascal] Gross is leading the line in regards to what goes on on the pitch and what is the right kind of way they want to play. And everybody's chipping in with goals. The look a very, very frightening team at the moment."
- Shades of Barca and Beckham - Brighton aim to maintain superb start 
  - Published1 day ago
- Timely recognition or long overdue? How Gross is proving all-time bargain 
  - Published10 October
Life after Welbeck
In the summer of 2025, Brighton lost their top scorer Joao Pedro to Chelsea, and history repeated itself this year when the Blues lured veteran forward Danny Welbeck to Stamford Bridge.
Once again, however, the Seagulls' enviable data-led recruitment model, aided by club owner Tony Bloom's close links to Jamestown Analytics, appears to have found a promising replacement.
Having been used primarily as a substitute last season, Greece striker Charalampos Kostoulas has been entrusted to spearhead the attack, and the 19-year-old has repaid the faith shown in him by Hurzeler with three league goals and two assists.
Only Lamine Yamal has more goal involvements among teenagers in Europe's top five leagues this season.
Kostoulas has a strong supporting cast including Hinshelwood, Yasin Ayari, Malick Yalcouye and Maxim de Cuyper, not to mention a rejuvenated Pascal Gross pulling the strings from a deeper position.
With 11 league scorers already - while also being the beneficiaries of three own goals - Hurzeler's men are sharing the load impressively. As well as being the division's top scorers, Brighton have had the most shots on target and sit second for xG, shots and big chances.
In the top five European leagues, only Barcelona, with 39 goals from nine La Liga matches, have more domestic league goals than Brighton.
Equally as encouraging is how well they have coped defensively despite the loss of centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke and midfield anchorman Carlos Baleba. Luka Vuskovic looks to be a tremendous acquisition from Tottenham Hotspur, and he has helped the Seagulls, who remain unbeaten at home, record a league-high five clean sheets.
- The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager 
  - Published3 days ago
What does history tell us?
There are only seven previous instances of a team scoring 23 or more goals after seven games of a Premier League season. All bar one have gone on to finish in the top three, with Manchester City winning the title in 2011-12 and 2022-23.
The outlier? Kevin Keegan's Newcastle United team of 1994-95, who faded and finished sixth. Comparisons have already been drawn between that side, dubbed 'The Entertainers', and the swagger of the current Brighton squad.
With that in mind, Alan Wares co-host of the Albion Roar podcast suggested that perhaps a Champions League place, rather than a full-blown title challenge, might be a more realistic aim.
"I think with the Premier League being seven games in and the other matches we've already played, I think the dream for us is sustainability. I wouldn't go for a target, just as high as possible," said Alan.
"The club is really wanting to qualify for Champions League at the end of the season but yes, we've made a good start - are we title contenders? It's way too early to consider that. I would say that, at the moment, is fantasy stuff. But every football fan's got to have their dream and our point is, why not?
"If we can continue this, and that is the main point we've got to look at, if we can be sustainable in what we're doing and what we achieve, then yes. Why not? Go for the sky, see what happens."
With Conference League football to juggle, it seems improbable Brighton's squad can last the pace with the likes of Arsenal for the duration of the season. Leicester City, the last outsiders to lift the title, do provide some hope. They were eighth with 12 points after seven games of their memorable 2015-16 triumph.
The Manchester City question
There is a chance Brighton's final league position could be affected by matters off the pitch.
Last month, an independent commission found Manchester City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-season period.
City are appealing against the verdict, meaning the severity and timing of any punishment - which could take the form of a points deduction - remain unknown.
Brighton have the chance to give City a fright when they travel to the Etihad on Halloween - one of four successive away games in all competitions - and the league table may well present a very different picture by the time November's international break comes around.
For now, Brighton are exactly where they deserve to be. And they're having great fun in the process.

title: People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
summary: People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days. Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a sma...
content:
People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.
The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.
Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates, sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”
Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.
The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman, a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.
Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.
It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.
Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.
Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.
“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.
Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.
Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.
Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

title: Haaland a doubt, Semenyo out - what are Man City's options?
summary: Haaland a doubt, Semenyo out - what are Man City's options? - Published Manchester City face the prospect of being without star striker Erling Haaland for Tuesday's Champions League game against AEK Athens. The Norway international scored twice in Saturday's 3-2 victory over Ipswich Town to take his...
content:
Haaland a doubt, Semenyo out - what are Man City's options?
- Published
Manchester City face the prospect of being without star striker Erling Haaland for Tuesday's Champions League game against AEK Athens.
The Norway international scored twice in Saturday's 3-2 victory over Ipswich Town to take his tally to eight Premier League goals for the season, leading the top-flight scoring charts once more.
But the 26-year-old suffered a blow to the foot in the game and is now a doubt for the European night at Etihad Stadium, as City look to get back to winning ways in the competition after last week's 4-2 defeat by Paris St-Germain.
"To replace Erling is always difficult but we have some different options," said manager Enzo Maresca. "It also depends on the gameplan.
"At the moment it is Erling. Why do we need to think of a different nine if Erling is there? If something happened or we need a different nine plan, we'll see."
Should Haaland not make a recovery, it would leave Maresca with a dilemma on who to select up front after Antoine Semenyo was ruled out for eight weeks with the left knee injury he picked up in the win over Ipswich.
- Boos and bananas on day of defiance at Man City 
  - Published2 days ago
False nine Foden?
Haaland has scored in six consecutive top-flight games to help City to the top of the table with a flawless start from their opening seven games of the campaign.
Against Ipswich, he scored his 100th non-penalty goal in the Premier League, reaching this milestone in fewer appearances than any other player.
Maresca said Haaland "can be available" against AEK and will be assessed after training on Monday, but the player was not present during the session which was open to the media.
Players can find it difficult to feature as back-ups to Haaland, as Julian Alvarez and Omar Marmoush have found in the past, but it was a surprise when Divin Mubama was allowed to join Championship side Southampton on loan in the summer.
It left City without a natural replacement in Haaland's absence.
Maresca has previously said Semenyo can be used "as a nine" but that plan is no longer available with the Ghanaian facing the prospect of missing up to 13 matches.
One option mooted by the Italian is midfielder Phil Foden, who ended his barren run in front of goal on Saturday by scoring his first Premier League goal since December.
"Phil can be one of the solutions," said Maresca. "He played already in the past in that position so could play again, but at the moment the number nine is Erling."
Could summer signing Iliman Ndiaye be another option?
The Senegal international was often deployed as a striker in Sheffield United's promotion-winning campaign in 2022-23, scoring 14 goals to help the Blades return to the Premier League.
Last season, manager Pep Guardiola said Rayan Cherki fits playing in the false nine role "perfectly", with the Frenchman scoring in a 2-0 Carabao Cup quarter-final win over Brentford when used in that position.
'Not good' losing Semenyo
Semenyo's injury complicates matters.
The City forward appeared as a 77th-minute substitute on Saturday but hobbled straight down the tunnel at full-time with Maresca initially expecting an "even worse injury".
The Ghana international has made 10 appearances in all competitions this season, scoring two goals and providing three assists.
"To lose Antoine or any player is not good," Maresca said on Monday.
"In the first moment we expected an even worse injury, so we were more worried, but after Sunday's scan we feel much better.
"It could be eight weeks. The most important thing for him is to recover and also when he is back, probably around December, we will have a new player in terms of energy.
"It is a collateral [knee injury], something like this. It is not a muscle problem."
Jeremy Doku started on the left flank against Ipswich and should continue in that role in the absence of Semenyo.

title: Tricky time for lunchboxes: banana shortage hits supermarket shelves after cool weather in Queensland
summary: A shortage of Australia’s most popular fruit, bananas, has hit supermarket shelves at a tricky time for lunchboxes, right as apple season winds down after tough growing conditions and summer stone fruit is yet to arrive en masse. Cool weather in key Queensland growing regions has severely slowed ban...
content:
A shortage of Australia’s most popular fruit, bananas, has hit supermarket shelves at a tricky time for lunchboxes, right as apple season winds down after tough growing conditions and summer stone fruit is yet to arrive en masse.
Cool weather in key Queensland growing regions has severely slowed banana production, leaving major supermarkets Coles, Woolworths and Aldi with sparse displays or very green stock.
Anton van den Berg, co-founder of the grocery delivery service Box Divvy, said demand for bananas has not fallen as significantly as it typically does for produce when supply drops.
“Many people will buy bananas no matter what, and so the demand is not adjusting, leading to shortages,” he said.
Van den Berg said major supermarkets have kept demand elevated because they rarely charge more than $5 a kilo to avoid putting off shoppers, and instead rely on thousands of other grocery lines to maintain profits.
In a note to shoppers, Woolworths said: “Recent weather in far north Queensland has slowed the growth of bananas. Stock may be limited this week, but fresh stock is arriving daily.”
Coles was contacted for comment.
Bananas are the most frequently bought fruit in Australia, according to produce data company Freshlogic, with almost nine in 10 households regularly buying them.
Apples are the next most popular fruit.
While cool weather has slowed banana growth just as the tropical fruit needs heat, unseasonably hot conditions have disrupted the temperate climates required by apple orchards, compounding the squeeze on favoured fruit.
Many countries are experiencing strains on their banana supplies but for very different reasons.
The US has reported supply strains caused by high transport fuel costs from the war with Iran, which has affected the long-distance, refrigerated shipping required to import bananas.
While the US relies on imports, Australia grows all of its own bananas across the northern areas of Queensland, Northern Territory and Western Australia.
The Australian lunchbox conundrum may prove short-lived, with expectations banana supplies will promptly rebound.
The Australian Banana Growers’ Council said “any shortage should soon correct itself” because temperatures across affected growing regions were beginning to rise.
In the meantime, prices for stone fruit, including peaches and nectarines, are expected to drop in the coming weeks as they come into season.
Fruit sellers are still reporting healthy stock levels of navel oranges and mandarins, both of which typically start to reduce in late spring, while mango quantities are rising.
Van den Berg said mango prices were already reducing quickly and may be a suitable, albeit messier, lunchbox alternative to bananas.
“There are some kids who only eat bananas, or will only eat pink lady apples, and parents don’t have much of a choice,” he said.
“But if you do, then mangoes are definitely a better option at the moment.”

title: Supreme Court to hear a new case on race and school admissions, this time in Maryland
summary: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to hear a new challenge to school admissions policies aimed at fostering diversity, taking up a case targeting a lottery-based process for magnet programs in a Maryland county. The court agreed to take up an appeal brought by the Association for Educat...
content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to hear a new challenge to school admissions policies aimed at fostering diversity, taking up a case targeting a lottery-based process for magnet programs in a Maryland county.
The court agreed to take up an appeal brought by the Association for Education Fairness seeking to revive a lawsuit it filed against the Montgomery County Board of Education. Montgomery County is a large and diverse county in the suburbs of Washington.
The challengers argue that a policy in Montgomery County's STEM and humanities magnet schools unfairly elevates Black and Latino students for admission in violation of the 14th Amendment. In 2023, the Supreme Court cited the same amendment in striking down the use of race in college admissions. But this case is narrower, asking the justices to decide a more technical question of what evidence challengers need to bring such a claim, so the court is not poised to issue a ruling on the constitutional issue.
The policy in question concerns a group of four middle schools with magnet programs.
The current programs are entered via lottery, a system introduced during the Covid pandemic. Entry to the lottery is based on how well students perform on tests when ranked against others in their schools, which the plaintiffs say adversely affects Asian students in high-performing schools. The challengers have targeted that process, as well as one first introduced in 2017 (which has been discontinued) that sought to increase enrollment of children in low-poverty areas.
That program, sparked by a report that said Black and Latino students were underrepresented and Asian students overrepresented in the middle school magnet programs in Montgomery County schools, included outreach to students and a cognitive test.
The plaintiffs say both programs were explicitly aimed at increasing Black and Latino enrollment, thereby violating the Constitution’s 14th Amendment.

title: ¿Cómo de ricos son tus vecinos? El mapa de la renta de los españoles, calle a calle
summary: ¿Cómo de ricos son tus vecinos? El mapa de la renta de los españoles, calle a calle Los nuevos datos del INE, de 2024, permiten ver la renta de los hogares en más de 30.000 secciones censales, cómo se reparte en cada municipio y cuánto ha cambiado desde 2019 La renta mediana por unidad de consumo si...
content:
¿Cómo de ricos son tus vecinos? El mapa de la renta de los españoles, calle a calle
Los nuevos datos del INE, de 2024, permiten ver la renta de los hogares en más de 30.000 secciones censales, cómo se reparte en cada municipio y cuánto ha cambiado desde 2019
La renta mediana por unidad de consumo siguió creciendo en 2024 en la gran mayoría de las secciones censales de España, la unidad estadística más pequeña, donde viven unas 1.500 personas. Entre 2019 y 2024 la renta aumentó en términos nominales en casi todas las más de 33.600 que hay en el país, pero en una de cada cinco el aumento no bastó para compensar la inflación acumulada del periodo, que fue del 18,8%. Es decir, en esas zonas los ingresos subieron menos que los precios y, por tanto, los hogares perdieron poder adquisitivo.
En el mapa a continuación puede consultar los datos más recientes disponibles de la renta mediana por unidad de consumo, casi calle a calle. Son datos del Atlas de distribución de renta de los hogares que publica anualmente el Instituto Nacional de Estadística.
Cargando
La renta mediana por unidad de consumo de los hogares es una métrica que tiene en cuenta todos los ingresos familiares y cuántos miembros hay en el hogar. Se calcula en dos pasos: primero se suman todos los ingresos; después se dividen por el número de personas, de manera ponderada (el primer adulto cuenta como una persona; el resto de mayores de 13 años computan como 0,5; y los de menos de esa edad, como 0,3).
Esto permite comparar diferentes tipos de familias: no es lo mismo una pareja que ingresa 3.000 euros al mes, que un núcleo en el que además de una pareja conviven otros dos niños y un adulto dependiente. La renta media de una sección puede variar de golpe solo con la llegada o partida de una familia de renta muy alta.
¿Cómo se distribuye la renta?
Los datos del Atlas permiten también analizar cómo se distribuye la renta dentro de cada municipio: qué proporción de los vecinos vive en las zonas más ricas y qué proporción en las más pobres. Una forma de medirlo es ver cómo se reparten las secciones censales del municipio según su renta. Para ello dividimos el conjunto de las secciones del país en diez grupos del mismo tamaño (deciles): el primero reúne el 10% de secciones con menor renta mediana y el décimo, el 10% con mayor renta.
En el siguiente buscador se pueden consultar los 6.711 municipios con datos y comparar la distribución de sus secciones tanto con la escala nacional como con la autonómica.
Así, en Madrid llama la atención el peso de las zonas de renta alta: el 36% de sus secciones censales está en el decil más rico de España, frente a solo un 7% en el más pobre. Sevilla muestra una distribución más polarizada, con un 19% de sus secciones en el decil más pobre y un 16% en el más rico. En Tarragona, los dos extremos pesan lo mismo: un 17% en cada uno.
El resultado cambia según la escala elegida: si las secciones de Madrid se comparan solo con las del resto de la comunidad, el 12% de ellas queda en el decil autonómico de menor renta.
Más ricos y más pobres
En el mapa se observan a simple vista varios polos de renta alta —en azul— localizados en las grandes áreas metropolitanas del país, principalmente en Madrid y Barcelona. De los 702 vecindarios con una renta mediana por unidad de consumo superior a 37.500 euros, 409 estaban en Madrid capital y Barcelona y otros 166 en municipios de su entorno, como Pozuelo de Alarcón o Sant Cugat del Vallès.
Con respecto a los datos del anterior Atlas, de 2023, la lista de los diez municipios más ricos apenas ha cambiado de orden, pero siguen siendo los mismos diez.
En el mapa también se identifican otras grandes urbes con zonas en rojo intenso que indican rentas mucho menores, aunque menos concentradas. Si analizamos los 896 vecindarios de menor renta —hasta 12.950 euros de renta mediana por unidad de consumo—, destacan ciudades del sur y el este del país, como Sevilla, con 59 secciones; Alicante, con 43; y Málaga, con 28. También aparece Madrid, con 27 secciones entre las de menor renta del país. El listado también es igual que el año pasado: ha entrado un distrito de Elda, en Alicante, en lugar de Beas de Segura, en Jaén.
Nota metodológica. Los datos de Navarra y Álava no aparece la variación desde 2019 porque sus series comparables para este indicador comienzan en 2021 y 2020, respectivamente.
En los valores extremos, el INE agrupa los valores: las rentas más bajas figuran como 8.050 euros y las más altas como 47.250 euros. Son límites estadísticos, no valores exactos.

title: High spirits: Supreme Court to decide fate of federal ban on home distilling
summary: WASHINGTON — In a boost for those who want to make whiskey in their bathtubs or gin in their kitchens, the Supreme Court announced Monday it will consider whether to strike down a long-standing federal ban on distilling spirits at home. Although interest in the home distilling of hooch has continued...
content:
WASHINGTON — In a boost for those who want to make whiskey in their bathtubs or gin in their kitchens, the Supreme Court announced Monday it will consider whether to strike down a long-standing federal ban on distilling spirits at home.
Although interest in the home distilling of hooch has continued despite the 150-year-old ban, advocates hope the court will remove the threat of criminal sanctions, which can include a fine of up to $10,000 and a maximum sentence of five years in prison.
For decades, people have been able to make wine and beer at home for personal use without any penalties.
The distilling ban was enacted in 1868 in a bid to counter tax evasion by those making spirits. It bars the distilling of spirits in “any dwelling house” or surrounding structures.
The challengers include the Hobby Distillers Association and several of its members. One, Scott McNutt, has a still at home that he has used to distill fuel alcohol. Another, Rick Morris, owns a company that manufactures stills that can be used at home.
They sued in Texas after being told by the federal Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau, part of the Treasury Department, that they could not obtain a license to distill at home because of the federal ban.
The lawsuit contains several claims, including that Congress exceeded its taxing power by passing a ban that did not actually raise any revenue.
In a separate challenge brought in Ohio, another would-be home distiller, John Ream, raised similar claims.
The two cases resulted in conflicting rulings by federal appeals courts. In the Texas case, the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals backed the challengers, while in the Ohio case, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reached the opposite conclusion.

As a result, both losing parties appealed, and all parties agreed the Supreme Court should issue a definitive ruling that would apply nationwide.
If the challengers win, they would still have to register their stills and pay excise tax on the spirits they produce, even though it would be for their own consumption.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer, representing the federal government, defended the law in court papers, saying that it is within the power of Congress to restrict taxable activities by location if there is a strong chance the taxes will not be paid.
Similar to marijuana, which remains broadly illegal under federal law while various states have legalized it, several states allow home distilling, including West Virginia, which legalized it in 2024. Those laws do not take precedence over the federal ban.
Legislation has also been introduced in Congress to repeal the federal restrictions.

title: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
summary: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal it later withdrew. The court action removes one barrier to Mohammed standing trial before a military commission in 2028, whe...
content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal brought by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged 9/11 plotters seeking to hold the government to a plea deal it later withdrew.
The court action removes one barrier to Mohammed standing trial before a military commission in 2028, where the death penalty is a possible punishment. He has been held at the U.S. base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.
Mohammed is accused of being the ringleader of the plot to crash hijacked planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania.
The other two men who appealed to the Supreme Court were Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash, who are also held at Guantanamo and set to face trial.
The three men had agreed to a plea deal with military prosecutors in 2024, signed off on by a military commission judge, that would have given them life sentences.
But days later, then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rejected the proposal, saying he had the authority to override the deal.

title: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review
summary: Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently. The company updated its guidelin...
content:
Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently.
The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content.
“Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as ‘nudification’ — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post.
Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review.
The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children.
Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users and removed 193,000 developer accounts due to fraud and abuse.
In July, the city of San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps, some of which were rated as suitable for minors.

title: Musk pledges to give ‘every kid in America’ one of his SpaceX shares
summary: Elon Musk claims he will give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” in 2027, which would result in a gift worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price of his combination spaceflight and AI company. That’s roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth. It’s not clear how M...
content:
Elon Musk claims he will give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” in 2027, which would result in a gift worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price of his combination spaceflight and AI company. That’s roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth.
It’s not clear how Musk plans to do this, though he said in a separate post that he wants to give the shares “directly to the public,” and that this will be the “first of many” shares he’ll donate.
President Donald Trump, who Musk spent around $300 million to help elect, has set up bank accounts for children through the Treasury, called Trump Accounts, that can accept stock donations from wealthy donors.
Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Musk’s post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new “public benefit fund,” which it intends to use to make “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” after its upcoming IPO.
On Sunday afternoon, Musk replied directly to Anthropic’s post on X about its new fund, suggesting the company should give “directly to the public” instead.
“This is what I will be doing,” he wrote in another reply four hours later. Then, overnight, he announced his plans to donate SpaceX stock.
There are currently more than 70 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics. Musk owns around 849 million Class A common shares of SpaceX and more than 5.5 billion Class B supervoting shares. He stands to earn many more.
Musk’s philanthropic giving to date has been almost exclusively done through his Musk Foundation. Despite his negative opinions about philanthropy, it’s the fifth-largest private charitable foundation in the U.S. However, a recent review by The Economist showed that a majority of the total money laid out by the Musk Foundation over the years has gone to entities tied to Musk in some way. Nearly 60% has gone to another charity, called The Foundation, run by his money manager, Jared Birchall.

title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
summary: If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real worl...
content:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon, October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto and a major Japanese automotive manufacturer.
Laplace is also working with Nvidia and T-Mobile on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation.

title: La conmoción en Australia después de que un vehículo arrollara y dejara gravemente herida a una diputada en un presunto ataque deliberado
summary: La conmoción en Australia después de que un vehículo arrollara y dejara gravemente herida a una diputada en un presunto ataque deliberado - Autor, Redacción - Título del autor, BBC News Mundo - Fecha de publicación - Tiempo de lectura: 3 min La diputada australiana Helen Haines resultó gravemente he...
content:
La conmoción en Australia después de que un vehículo arrollara y dejara gravemente herida a una diputada en un presunto ataque deliberado
  - Autor, Redacción
  - Título del autor, BBC News Mundo
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 3 min
La diputada australiana Helen Haines resultó gravemente herida tras un presunto ataque en el que se vio involucrado un vehículo, ocurrido frente a su oficina electoral en Wangaratta, una ciudad situada pocas horas al noreste de Melbourne, en el estado de Victoria.
Haines se encontraba en un estacionamiento cerca de su oficina cuando fue alcanzada por una camioneta todoterreno.
El primer ministro, Anthony Albanese, confirmó que un hombre se encuentra bajo custodia tras el incidente y que, por el momento, se desconocen los motivos del presunto ataque.
"No fue un accidente. Al parecer, se trató de un acto deliberado", declaró al programa "730" de la cadena ABC.
"Esperamos, sin duda, recibir buenas noticias sobre el estado de Helen en las próximas 24 horas", agregó.
Albanese señaló que la policía antiterrorista examinará los antecedentes del sospechoso para tratar de determinar sus motivos.
Y añadió que, desde hace tiempo, viene pidiendo que se rebaje la tensión en el ámbito político.
"Si uno observa las redes sociales de cualquier persona y lee los comentarios, se encuentra con afirmaciones que nadie se atrevería a hacer cara a cara. La tensión ha aumentado, y no solo aquí en Australia; también hemos sido testigos de incidentes similares a nivel internacional", dijo.
"En una democracia, no hay lugar para la violencia".
Por su parte, el primer ministro del estado australiano de Victoria, Ben Carroll, dijo sentirse "profundamente consternado" por este "ataque violento".
"Sé lo devastador que resultará esto para la comunidad de Wangaratta y para todas las personas a quienes Helen representa", comentó.
El líder de la oposición en Australia, Angus Taylor, afirmó sentirse "profundamente entristecido y consternado" por la noticia.
"Rezo por Helen y pienso en su familia y sus seres queridos. Es un día estremecedor para nuestra nación. Nadie debería ser objeto de un ataque de este tipo".
"Nuestro país no puede convertirse en un lugar donde se normalicen los ataques violentos", comentó.
El sospechoso
La policía de Victoria informó que un hombre de 43 años fue detenido después de que Helen Haines fuera atropellada por un vehículo cerca de su oficina en Wangaratta.
Se sabe que el hombre es oriundo de Tarrawingee, una localidad cercana en el estado de Victoria.
Conducía un Toyota Land Cruiser de color blanco. Se encontró un cuchillo dentro del vehículo.
El sospechoso fue interceptado en el lugar de los hechos por un transeúnte, antes de quedar bajo custodia policial.
¿Quién es Helen Haines?
Helen Haines es una diputada independiente de 65 años que representa a la circunscripción de Indi, en el estado de Victoria, en el sureste de Australia.
Fue elegida por primera vez para la Cámara de Representantes de Australia en 2019, y resultó reelegida en 2022 y 2025.
Antes de dedicarse a la política, trabajó como enfermera, partera e investigadora en el ámbito de la salud pública.
Ha publicado varios trabajos de investigación sobre salud materna.
Tras el incidente, la familia de Haines hizo la siguiente declaración:
"Esta tarde, nuestra querida Helen se ha visto involucrada en un incidente a las puertas de su oficina electoral en Wangaratta y está recibiendo atención médica.
Agradecemos la rápida intervención de las personas que se encontraban en el lugar, la labor de los profesionales sanitarios que la atendieron y la respuesta de la policía.
Ni nuestra familia ni el equipo de Helen haremos más comentarios por el momento, y solicitamos que tanto el público como los medios de comunicación respeten nuestra privacidad. Por favor, tengan a Helen presente en sus pensamientos".

title: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
summary: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks Scientists discovered that dying corals can recover in record time simply by touching healthy clones, opening a promising new path to saving threatened reefs. - Date: - October 19, 2026 - Source: - Stanford Doerr School of Sustainabi...
content:
A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
Scientists discovered that dying corals can recover in record time simply by touching healthy clones, opening a promising new path to saving threatened reefs.
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. In laboratory experiments, dying corals regained their color and fully recovered within seven weeks, with as little as five days of contact sometimes enough to start the healing process.
- Share:
For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that severely bleached corals can fully recover after spending just a few days in contact with healthy, genetically identical corals.
In laboratory experiments, corals that had turned white and were close to dying regained their health within seven weeks. According to a study published on October 14 in Science Advances, this represents the fastest documented recovery from coral bleaching. The discovery could lead to new techniques for restoring coral reefs, which some estimates suggest could disappear within decades as climate change fuels increasingly severe and frequent marine heat waves.
Coral bleaching occurs when rising ocean temperatures cause corals to lose the beneficial algae living inside their tissues. These algae supply much of the energy corals depend on for growth and survival. Without them, corals lose their vibrant colors, struggle to obtain enough nourishment, and become more susceptible to harmful algae. Even when they survive, regaining their health can take months or years.
"While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," said lead author Danny Collins, an oceans PhD student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. "The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?"
An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a Way to Rescue Dying Corals
Although they may resemble plants or rocks, corals are animals. In most coral species, individual animals reproduce by creating genetically identical copies of themselves. These clones grow together into large colonies that form the foundation of coral reefs.
The idea for the study emerged from an unexpected observation in 2025. Steve Palumbi, a study coauthor and the Jane and Marshall Steel, Jr. Professor in Marine Sciences, noticed something unusual in his laboratory. Two fragments taken from the same coral colony, one healthy and the other bleached, had fallen against each other in an aquarium.
Where the fragments touched, the bleached coral began regaining its color. The change suggested that beneficial algae were returning to its tissues.
At roughly the same time, Collins was investigating how coral diseases develop and spread. He was particularly interested in bacteria carried by plastic debris that lands on corals and can introduce harmful microorganisms through direct contact.
"Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact," said Collins, who is also a Knight-Hennessy Scholar. "We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good - the beneficial algae from healthy corals."
To investigate, Collins designed an experiment using 10 pairs of coral fragments. Each pair consisted of one healthy fragment and one bleached fragment originating from the same coral animal.
Five pairs were positioned so that the fragments physically touched. The other five pairs were separated by gaps measuring only a few millimeters.
The results revealed a dramatic difference. Every bleached fragment that touched its healthy counterpart recovered completely within seven weeks. In contrast, the bleached fragments that were kept apart died.
How a Simple Touch Triggers Rapid Coral Recovery
The researchers discovered that the remarkable recovery depends on a special ability of genetically identical corals to connect their tissues.
"Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact," said Palumbi, who is a professor of oceans in the Doerr School of Sustainability and of biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences. "Their tissues fuse if they are from the same clone. We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin."
Using a powerful microscope, Collins and his colleagues examined what happened when the coral fragments touched. They found that tiny channels within their tissues quickly lined up, forming connections that allowed materials to move between the two fragments.
Through these connections, beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce could pass from the healthy coral into the bleached one. Within just three days, researchers observed algae transferring into the damaged fragments.
The team then investigated how long the corals actually needed to remain connected. By separating pairs after different periods of contact, they discovered that a single week was enough to transfer the algae required for complete recovery. In some cases, just five days of contact produced the same result.
Remarkably, the separated corals still returned to full health within seven weeks, the same amount of time required by corals that remained connected throughout the experiment.
This finding revealed that the rapid recovery was not primarily driven by a continuing supply of algae from the healthy coral. Instead, once enough algae entered the bleached fragment, they reproduced rapidly inside their new host and restored its energy supply.
"Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don't just spread out," said Palumbi. "They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals."

title: Astronomers discover a ghostly green star unlike any known before
summary: Astronomers discover a ghostly green star unlike any known before Astronomers have discovered the first known green star, revealing a hidden rainbow of dead stars glowing in colors once thought impossible. - Date: - October 19, 2026 - Source: - University of Warwick - Summary: - Astronomers have unc...
content:
Astronomers discover a ghostly green star unlike any known before
Astronomers have discovered the first known green star, revealing a hidden rainbow of dead stars glowing in colors once thought impossible.
- Date:
- October 19, 2026
- Source:
- University of Warwick
- Summary:
- Astronomers have uncovered a surprising rainbow of dead stars, including the first known star that would appear genuinely green to human eyes. Researchers found that white dwarfs can glow in unexpected shades of pink, purple, yellow, and cyan because of unusual chemical interactions in their extremely dense atmospheres.
- Share:
Astronomers at the University of Warwick have discovered that white dwarf stars can display a surprising variety of colors, including green, pink, purple, yellow, and cyan. Among their findings is the first known star that would appear genuinely green to the human eye.
For most stars, color is closely tied to temperature. Cooler stars appear orange, stars like our Sun look white, and the hottest stars shine pale blue. The relationship is similar to heating a piece of iron, which changes from red to orange and eventually white as its temperature rises.
White dwarfs, the extremely dense remains of stars similar to our Sun, were long believed to follow this same pattern. In fact, they received their name because the first examples discovered were unusually hot and appeared white or pale blue. However, scientists have now found that these stellar remnants can produce a much broader spectrum of colors.
The findings, published in RAS Techniques and Instruments (RASTI), suggest that some white dwarfs would look dramatically different from ordinary stars if they could be viewed from close enough.
"Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," said Dr. Mark Hollands, Warwick Prize Fellow in the Astronomy and Astrophysics Group, University of Warwick, who led the work. "It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me."
Why Some Dead Stars Glow in Unexpected Colors
The explanation lies in the extraordinary density of white dwarf atmospheres. In the coolest of these stars, atmospheric material can reach densities of approximately 1 gram per cubic centimeter, comparable to water and millions of times denser than the Sun's visible surface, known as the photosphere.
Under these extreme conditions, small amounts of elements such as carbon, calcium, and sodium interact with the surrounding helium plasma. These interactions allow the elements to absorb a much wider range of light wavelengths than they would in less dense environments.
As a result, the light escaping from a white dwarf can take on colors that would not normally be expected based on temperature alone. Instead of appearing orange, white, or blue, some of these stars develop entirely different hues.
Because no white dwarf is close enough for astronomers to directly distinguish its color with the human eye, the researchers used measurements of starlight to determine how each star would appear.
They analyzed stellar spectra, which are produced by separating light into its component wavelengths, much as a prism divides sunlight into the colors of a rainbow. Each spectrum acts as a distinctive fingerprint, revealing information about a star's temperature and chemical composition.
By processing these measurements through a model of human color vision, the team calculated the colors that people would actually perceive. This approach demonstrated that spectral data can reveal not only what a star contains and how hot it is, but also its true visual appearance.
Astronomers Identify the First Known Green Star
When the researchers examined white dwarfs throughout the sky, they found that the stars could be divided into several color groups based on the chemical makeup of their atmospheres.
White dwarfs containing large amounts of carbon often appear pink or purple. Others that have accumulated material from destroyed asteroids and comets, remnants of planetary systems that once surrounded them, tend to look yellow.
Cooler white dwarfs with atmospheres containing both hydrogen and helium can develop cyan or pale blue coloring. This effect occurs when hydrogen molecules collide with helium atoms under the immense pressures found in these stars.
Perhaps the most remarkable discovery was WD J1330+6435, a white dwarf with a temperature of approximately 4,000 degrees Celsius.
Over time, this star has drawn in rocky debris from its former planetary system, introducing calcium, lithium, and sodium into its atmosphere. According to the researchers' calculations, these elements give the star a distinctive chartreuse green appearance.
As far as the team knows, no other star, whether still undergoing nuclear fusion or already dead, has ever been credibly identified as genuinely green. This makes WD J1330+6435 the first known example of a green star in the Milky Way.
Dr. Hollands added: "The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow. Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction."
A Dead Star That May Be the Reddest Ever Found
At the other end of the color spectrum, the astronomers identified another extraordinary white dwarf that may be the reddest star ever documented.
Known as WD J1011+2845, this stellar remnant is located just 48 light-years from Earth. It has a deep convection zone that transports carbon from its interior to its surface.
Once there, carbon molecules dramatically alter the wavelengths of light escaping from the star. Nearly all of its light is shifted toward wavelengths longer than 600 nanometers, producing an unusually deep salmon-pink appearance.

title: Everton legend Ferguson returns to management in Irish League
summary: Ferguson named boss of Irish League club Glentoran - Published Former Everton and Rangers striker Duncan Ferguson has sensationally been named as the new manager of Irish Premiership club Glentoran. The 54-year-old, who also played for Dundee United and Newcastle United and won seven caps for Scotla...
content:
Ferguson named boss of Irish League club Glentoran
- Published
Former Everton and Rangers striker Duncan Ferguson has sensationally been named as the new manager of Irish Premiership club Glentoran.
The 54-year-old, who also played for Dundee United and Newcastle United and won seven caps for Scotland, will take up the reins at the east Belfast club on what the club say is a "multi-year contract".
Ferguson's coaching career to date includes being assistant manager at Everton under renowned managers Carlo Ancelotti and Rafael Benitez, and also two spells as caretaker boss.
In recent years, he has managed Forest Green Rovers and Inverness Caledonian Thistle.
Ferguson's surprise appointment follows the departure of Declan Devine as manager of the Irish League outfit in September.
His former Dundee United team-mate Gary Bollan, with whom he worked at Inverness, has been named as assistant manager.
Glentoran have not won a league title since 2009 despite significant investment from owner Ali Pour and the adoption of a full-time professional model in recent years.
"I am delighted to become manager of Glentoran," said Ferguson, whose first game as boss will be at home to Ballymena United on Saturday (15:00 BST).
"This is a big club with a tremendous history, and it is a great opportunity for me. I understand the responsibility that comes with the job.
"I want to win trophies here. Glentoran should be challenging for the title and every cup and shield we enter. I know that success here will be judged on what we win.
"The more I spoke with Ali and Paul [Millar, sporting director], the more I wanted the job. Their ambition matches my own, and I am looking forward to getting onto the training pitch, working with the players and seeing what we can achieve together."
- I'll give Glens everything, vows new boss Ferguson 
  - Published9 hours ago
- What awaits Everton hero Ferguson in shock Glens role? 
  - Published1 day ago
- Ferguson link has caused a 'real buzz' - McCann 
  - Published2 days ago
'We took the time this decision deserved'
Ferguson, who also worked under Roberto Martinez and Ronald Koeman at Everton, added that he has "signed for the long term".
"I want to get to know the people at the Club and in the wider community and become part of life here. That is important to me," he said.
"I have heard so much about the Glentoran supporters and what this Club means to them. We have a responsibility to win games and make them proud. Their support has to be earned, and I am looking forward to getting started."
Glens owner Pour said Ferguson's appointment reflects the club's "ambition to win trophies".
"We took the time this decision deserved. We conducted a rigorous recruitment process, interviewing candidates from across the United Kingdom, Ireland and Scandinavia," added Pour.
"We carefully assessed their experience and proposals and completed our due diligence before making the appointment.
"Paul and I met Duncan on several occasions in Liverpool. Those conversations gave us the opportunity to explore his approach to management, discuss the demands of the role and understand what he could contribute to Glentoran.
"His football knowledge, experience and determination to take on this opportunity impressed us. Duncan demonstrated the qualities we were looking for in coaching, leadership, player development and recruitment, supported by strong relationships across the game."
'I still can't believe it' - Leeman
Former Glentoran captain Paul Leeman, who played 597 games for the club, is excited at the prospect of Ferguson in the Oval dugout.
"I still can't believe it - it's a huge appointment and I'm interested to see his plans for Glentoran," Leeman told BBC Radio Ulster.
"It is a risk and he's been known more as a number two. But he has bags of experience in football. He's worked at the top, top level and there's certainly something he can add to the team.
"He doesn't know the league so I think he has to have people around him who do.
"He's coming to the Irish League to probably try to resurrect his own managerial career. He will demand respect from the players straight away and it's certainly going to be interesting."
The Glens had been linked with a move to appoint former Northern Ireland international Jim Magilton, but the ex-Ipswich Town and Queens Park Rangers boss opted to remain with their Irish Premiership rivals Cliftonville.
Devine left by mutual consent after two and a half years at the helm.
The former Derry City and Bohemians boss guided the club to a County Antrim Shield success in the 2024-25 season, their first trophy triumph since lifting the Irish Cup in 2020.
Ferguson is now tasked with ending the long drought since the Glens' last league victory 17 years ago.
Glentoran sit third in the Irish Premiership standings, having won six and lost four of their first 12 league outings this season.

title: Cuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in Gaza
summary: This winter is likely to deepen hunger for Palestinians in Gaza, after sweeping aid cuts forced the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) to end support for more than half a million people each month, the agency’s director for Palestine said. More than a year after a Trump-brokered ceasefire came into for...
content:
This winter is likely to deepen hunger for Palestinians in Gaza, after sweeping aid cuts forced the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) to end support for more than half a million people each month, the agency’s director for Palestine said.
More than a year after a Trump-brokered ceasefire came into force, promised reconstruction has not begun, there are few jobs and the vast majority in Gaza still rely on aid to eat.
This summer, WFP programmes helped feed three-quarters of Gaza’s population, about 1.6 million people, but funding has fallen by more than half from 2025 levels.
As a result, from October, aid has been scaled back to 1.1 million people each month. Cuts to deliveries of ration boxes, cash stipends to buy food in markets, and hot meals at community kitchens have already been rolled out.
The WFP needs more than £300m over the next six months to restore and maintain critical programmes in Palestine.
A year of large aid shipments ended a famine declared in summer 2025 and reduced the most severe hunger, but without steps to rebuild Gaza’s economy, most families still rely on food handouts.
“These are very fragile gains, easily reversed, and the situation is still brutal,” said Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s representative and country director for Palestine.
Two-thirds of the population in Gaza face crisis levels of food insecurity, phase three under the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), which is used to assess if a population is approaching famine.
Food insecurity is at emergency levels for 200,000 Palestinians, which means immediate humanitarian supplies are needed to prevent deaths from hunger, Hughes said. This is IPC phase four, one step away from famine conditions.
Young children and their mothers are particularly vulnerable. After enduring years of food shortages, one in eight children in Gaza are chronically malnourished or stunted, a recent Unicef survey found, and may have suffered permanent damage.
Most humanitarian organisations are struggling with funding after the Trump administration decimated USAID and other donor nations cut aid spending as they grapple with cost of living crises.
The famine and war brought global attention to Gaza last year, ensuring funding. With a nominal ceasefire in place and the most extreme malnutrition curbed, the crisis there has slipped out of headlines and fatigue has set in among many donors.
However aid will be needed at scale until Israel and the international community launch the large-scale reconstruction promised last year. There is no way for most people to feed their own families at present, because about 80% of Gaza’s population is unemployed, according to UN data.
“We need to invest in recovery. This humanitarian operation isn’t affordable or sustainable in the long term,” Hughes said. “Ultimately that’s also what everyone in Gaza is telling us. They really don’t want to be reliant on these handouts, don’t want to stand in the hot meals queue every day. They want to have some chance of stability and recovery.”
Gaza was self-sufficient in fruit and vegetables before the war, but the vast majority of farmland has been occupied by Israel’s military. The sophisticated greenhouse and irrigation systems that supported agricultural production have been destroyed.
Fish has historically been a key source of protein in the territory, but the Israeli navy bars fishing boats from waters off the coast.
Alaa Sarhan, 40, lives with his wife and five children aged between four and 16 in a tent near the “yellow line” the marker of Israeli control. They have already noticed the impact of the WFP cuts.
“In recent days, we have had to plan our meals around what is available rather than what we want to eat,” he said. A former paramedic, he was injured by Israeli attacks nearly two decades ago, and his disability benefits buy very little.
“Often, I give up my share of food so my children can eat. I got accustomed to doing this because the most important thing is that they have something to eat.”
For three years, Israeli restrictions on aid shipments have been the main driver of hunger and malnutrition in Gaza. For months at a time, entry of food was restricted or entirely barred as Palestinians went hungry inside the territory.
Now, for the first time since October 2023, lack of funds may also become an obstacle to feeding hungry Palestinians. Israel’s controls on shipments into Gaza exacerbate funding shortfalls, because they make humanitarian work particularly expensive compared with other parts of the world.
Limits on fuel, engine oil and spare parts, and complex, opaque shipping restrictions push up transport time and costs. Mass destruction of buildings by airstrikes means warehouse space is limited and costly.
Even an influx of cash might not allow the WFP to immediately reverse the cuts. Sourcing and shipping the ingredients for ration boxes can take about three months, and the reduction of cash transfers may already be affecting supply chains.
The injection of more than £30m a month has “underpinned purchasing power for the private sector in Gaza”, Hughes said, allowing trucks to come in with relatively expensive shipments of both healthy and unhealthy food.
For now, the WFP has tried to reduce the impact of funding cuts by scaling back these programmes rather than cutting them entirely. Families who get ration boxes will receive one, rather than two.
But even limited reductions may push families with no other food source or income back into dangerous levels of malnutrition. For the poorest of the poor, reduced rations don’t work, Hughes said. “There’s only so far you can cut [support] until you don’t have the food security impact at the household level.”
The WFP is trying to monitor hunger levels so they reach the most vulnerable, monitoring “negative coping strategies”. These include whether people have skipped meals, or are seeking exploitative and dangerous work.

title: Three deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivals
summary: There is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country. Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in w...
content:
There is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country.
Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in western Japan, was carrying a giant float with other participants in a festival on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure, Agence France-Presse reported. Nabae, 62, was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said, adding that no one else was injured.
He died less than two weeks after a 51-year-old man was crushed beneath a wooden float he was riding at one of the annual Danjiri festivals held in southern Osaka prefecture. The same day, a 48-year-old man was killed in a similar accident at a Danjiri event in a nearby town. Police said 16 people were injured in the incidents.
The accidents occurred when the floats, which can weigh up to 4 tonnes, toppled as they were being pulled at speed around tight corners by hundreds of men, police said. The turns, known as yarimawashi, are a highlight of the festivals, originally held to pray for good autumn harvests.
It is not clear if Nabae lost his balance or if the contraption toppled on to him, according to police in Saijo, where the festival has been held annually since the Edo period (1603-1868).
Media reports said 11 floats, each weighing as much as 3 tonnes, were lined up side by side at the time of the accident.
The annual Saijo festivals, featuring more than 100 floats, are held to thank Shinto deities for plentiful grain crops, the Jiji news agency said.
Saijo’s mayor, Mitsuyoshi Ochi, voiced shock and sadness at Nabae’s death. “Just when we were about to work together to build a new administration for Saijo, this tragedy occurred. I still can’t believe it. I offer my heartfelt condolences,” he said in a statement.
In February, two people died in a crush at the “naked man festival” in Okayama, where as many as 10,000 men dressed in fundoshi loincloths squeeze into the grounds of a temple and compete to seize a pair of sacred wooden sticks thrown into the crowd by the head priest. The two men who succeed are declared “lucky men” for the year.
